text: Start with the evidence Carrick earned. He took over on 13 January after Ruben Amorim left and Darren Fletcher covered the following week. United collected thirty-nine league points from then to the finish, the best total in the division over that span, and ended third. It was not a miracle. It was a correction. Carrick returned the team to a flexible 4-2-3-1, put players in recognisable zones, moved Bruno Fernandes closer to the forward line, and defended in a compact 4-4-2. Imagine you are a centre-back facing them. If you step forward, United can release runners into the space behind you. If you sit off, Bruno can receive between your midfield and defence. The football became simpler, and confidence followed. That is a coaching achievement, not an illusion. The rescue also tells us what Carrick is good at. He reduced the number of decisions players had to make, gave the midfield a reliable first pass, and brought the forwards into the game earlier. That matters because confidence in football is often a consequence of structure rather than a mysterious mood. But the same simplification can become predictable when the opponent sits behind the ball. The rescue was real; it was simply narrower than the mythology around it.
